title: How Have We Lived So Long Without Portuguese Bubbles?
summary:
Historically, Portugal is one of the last places you’d expect to find Champagne-style wines, but the country's sparkling landscape has been evolving.

The post How Have We Lived So Long Without Portuguese Bubbles? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It was a revelatory shock. Ages ago, on my first-ever trip to Porto, I stood in a bottle shop, dumbfounded by the abundance of Portuguese traditional-method sparkling wines on the shelves. Why is Portuguese bubbly not a thing elsewhere? I wondered.

Historically, Portugal is one of the last places you’d expect to find Champagne-style wines. The average drinker is completely oblivious to the country’s high-quality traditional-method bottlings—they are the Mr. Cellophane to Vinho Verde’s Roxie Hart, for the Chicago fans out there. But the Portuguese sparkling landscape has been evolving, with producers slowly making international inroads here and there. And in what can still be a stubbornly patriarchal industry, it’s notably women winemakers who have been bubbling to the top.

From France With Love… And a Side of Sardines

The Portuguese realize the sparkling world still revolves around those chalky hills billowing out from Reims and Épernay. They’re not here to reinvent the wheel or claim the crown. They’re just trying to give Champagne’s venerable heritage an inimitable Lusophone accent.

It all began by the ocean, in the weather-beaten basin of Bairrada. Local lore holds that Napoleon’s troops introduced Champagne-method production to the area during their ill-fated invasion of Portugal in the early 1800s. The Portuguese-British alliance drove the French out in 1811, but it wasn’t until the 1890s that Portuguese wineries began producing sparkling wine on a commercial scale. Now, with all things fizz in fashion, and with Portugal’s international profile continuing to surge, the country’s overlooked traditional-method wines may finally have a fighting chance to carve out serious space in markets abroad.

The Other, Other Vinho Verde

North of Bairrada, in the corner of the country known for “green wine,” a revolution of sorts has been underway.

“Vinho Verde is not the obstacle. The simplification of it abroad is,” lamented Maria João Cerdeira, co-owner at Soalheiro in the far northern reaches of the Minho region. The inexpensive, fizzy style known to supermarket coldboxes worldwide—not that there’s anything wrong with it—has left the region a victim of its own mass-market success. “Vinho Verde is a diverse region, with distinct subregions, noble grape varieties, and the capacity to produce serious wines, including traditional-method sparkling,” she insisted.

Her family’s estate, a household name for still wines since 1974, raised the bar for regional fizz with Iberia’s first traditional-method Alvarinho back in 1995. Originally a veterinarian by trade, Cerdeira returned to work at the family business several years ago, and now oversees the entire operation. In 2024, another woman, the gifted Asun Carballo, ascended to lead the winemaking team, forming a formidable duo that is now pushing the winery toward new heights.

“What first caught my interest was not the [Champagne method] itself, but the idea that Alvarinho—a variety so deeply identified with our region as a still wine—could express itself in a completely different language,” Cerdeira said.

Other local varieties, like Loureiro and Azal, are more easily tamed into a balanced sparkling. With Alvarinho, it’s a tightrope walk to capture its special aromatic flamboyance while holding onto restraint and finesse. “For sparkling, we return to the roots of the variety: lower alcohol, lower pH, higher natural acidity, and more linearity,” she explained. “[It’s] a base wine that holds back, allowing time on lees to shape its complexity.”

Vinho Verde and the Minho region are coming of age, shedding the reputational shackles of cheap-and-cheerful supermarket wine and a patriarchal mentality. “We are seeing a new generation of women in Portuguese wine taking on leading roles, bringing a complementary sensibility—attention to detail, long-term thinking, and care for both people and place,” she said. “It’s not a coincidence, but neither is it a movement defined by gender. It reflects how the industry itself is evolving.”

Mining Portugal’s Mountainous Core

Meanwhile, to the southeast, Marta Lourenço is ensuring that Portugal’s most beloved traditional-method winery remains an icon. Wedged high in the mountains between Douro and Dão is a small region called Távora-Varosa, and its most famous winery, Murganheira, produces what many Portuguese call their “Champagne brand.” Bringing a bottle of Murganheira Super Reserva Bruto—with its instantly recognizable tuxedo-black-and-gold label—makes a statement in the average Portuguese household.

Sure, it’s only about 15 euros at the local supermarket. But in a country where the average spend for a local bottle is between five and 10 euros, that’s a splurge. Every time I’ve brought it to a party, even the wealthier, hardcore wine snobs hold out their glasses.

For almost 20 years now, Murganheira and its sister operation, Raposeira, have been lucky enough to have Lourenço calling the shots.

In the cellars and caves of Távora-Varosa, she and her team craft the flagship classics of Portugal’s only DOC that’s almost exclusively dedicated to traditional-method bubbly.

But that wasn’t her original plan.

“My life’s dream was quite different—to be an occupational therapist,” admitted Lourenço. “Since I didn’t achieve that, life naturally led me down this path.” And as if on cue, France made an entrance. “I soon understood that I had to travel to Champagne,” she said. “To ‘take the leap,’ because of the technique and know-how for rigor and excellence.”

While Lourenço will always be influenced by her time in Champagne, she maintains that her mountain region is unlike anything else. “In Távora-Varosa, we achieve the natural freshness of Champagne, but because we have more hours of sunshine, our grapes have superior aromatic maturation, which translates into our sparkling wines,” she said. “We have [some] that we harvest with 13.5% [potential alcohol], and they still arrive with 17 grams of acidity. That’s what makes us so special.”

Ambassador of the Central Coast

It’s easy to feel bad for the vines of Portugal’s central coast. They take a brutal beating from the Atlantic. “They told me when coming to Portugal that there is sun,” complained a fellow passenger on a recent visit with Daniel Niepoort, rising star of the celebrated Niepoort winemaking clan. “This isn’t Portugal,” Daniel replied. “This is Bairrada.”

It was a statement of both complaint and adoration.

The limestone-clay soils and ocean-lashed climate produce wines of incredible tension, salinity, and complexity. If traditional-method bottlings from Vinho Verde are the exuberant, expressive upstarts—and those from the mountains of Távora-Varosa the noble classics—Bairrada bubbly is quickly becoming the gastronomic darling of sommeliers worldwide. It’s why the region’s winemakers ironically embrace their moody kingdom by the sea.

A few days later, I arrived for an audience with Filipa Pato, a legend of Bairrada. While once known primarily as the daughter of Luís Pato, the region’s winemaking godfather, she—along with husband-partner William Wouters—has arguably risen to even greater heights through her unrelenting curiosity and biodynamic methodologies.

Leveraging the inherent balance and harmony of the local flora and fauna teases out wines of ethereal delicacy and detail. “Before climate change, Bairrada was not an easy region for still wines,” she said. “In many years, ripening was difficult. You maybe had two or three really good vintages per decade. So making high-quality sparkling wine was not only a stylistic choice; it was almost a natural necessity.”

Carving out a niche in the shadow of her father was no easy road, though. For years, the chemical engineer-turned-vigneron toiled in bare-bones, garagiste fashion—patiently learning and listening to what the terroir had to say. “I started in 2001 from scratch. There was no money, no property, no help from anyone. Only my grandmother, who gave me the opportunity to start in my grandfather’s old winery,” she recalled. “There was almost nothing, just walls.”

At the time, Bairrada was still a footnote on the global stage. Producers plied their craft and built slowly. Joining forces professionally in 2006 with William, a renowned Belgian sommelier and restaurateur, boosted their international visibility, and they rebranded as Filipa Pato & William Wouters. But that didn’t mean the challenges of being a female winemaker vanished overnight. “It wasn’t so easy,” she said. “As a woman in Portugal, you had to insist more—and in many ways, that’s still true today.”

Playing the Long Game

Nothing here—aside from cars and rent prices— moves fast. Lunches demand hours of commitment, conversations are epic sagas, wine is drunk slowly (if copiously), and getting the check quickly is nearly impossible.

Anything else would be wholly un-Portuguese.

Fittingly, international appreciation for the country’s traditional-method bubbly is growing gradually, modestly, and in baby steps. Like a friendship with the locals, it’s taking its own sweet, stubborn, frustrating time. But once embraced, you’ll wonder how the hell you’ve ever gotten along without them.

Bottles to Look For

Rich red berries and suave texture are grounded by racy acidity and subtle salinity in the estate’s brilliant entrylevel offering. Gastronomic and downright fun to drink.

Bringing classic scents of baked green apple, hazelnut, and brioche to go with a creamy texture and a centering core of citrus and mineral.

The peachy-floral glow of Alvarinho is tamed by crisp apple and tangerine-hued citrus, all anchored by a whisper of brioche and lick of wet stone.

Serves up dried orchard fruit and floral aromas with a side of rising dough, oyster shell, and saline minerality. Classy and poised while irresistibly expressive.

Offers citrus and light berry tones to go with silky bubbles and hints of toasted brioche and sea salt. Perfect as an aperitif.

title: Europe’s Next Great Chardonnay Hotspot Is Not Where You Think
summary:
The real story isn't simply that German Chardonnay has become better. It's that it stopped trying to be something else.

The post Europe’s Next Great Chardonnay Hotspot Is Not Where You Think appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For a week this spring, I reviewed more than 500 German wines, expecting Riesling to reaffirm why it remains the country’s defining white grape. Instead, somewhere between the familiar brilliance of Riesling and Germany’s increasingly accomplished Pinot Noirs, I found myself returning to Chardonnay.

Across Baden, Rheinhessen, the Pfalz, and beyond, quality was remarkably consistent. The wines combined freshness with texture, precision with generosity, and, perhaps most strikingly, all of the above with confidence. Having followed German wine for the past decade, I wasn’t surprised to find outstanding Chardonnay. What surprised me was how many producers had reached such an exceptional level.

The reasons why are both climatic and cultural. Warmer seasons have made ripening more reliable, while growers have become more exacting about where Chardonnay belongs. Older aromatic clones have given way to lower-yielding French selections, vineyards have matured, and a new generation of winemakers has returned from Burgundy and other wine regions with a sharper understanding of both vineyard and cellar.

“The vineyard is where great Chardonnay is made,” says Tobias Knewitz of Weingut Knewitz in Rheinhessen. “The cellar can’t create greatness, it can only preserve what the vineyard has already given us.”

That philosophy surfaced in nearly every conversation I had with German winemakers. Producers spoke of healthier soils, better site selection, spontaneous fermentation, longer lees ageing, and increasingly restrained oak. All are in service of expressing place rather than technique. Climate change has undoubtedly helped Chardonnay ripen more consistently in German wine regions, but it has also shifted the challenge toward preserving freshness while navigating frequent spring frosts.

Yet, after speaking with producers and sommeliers, I realized that the real story isn’t simply that German Chardonnay has become better. It’s that it stopped trying to be something else.

“We don’t want to make Burgundy in Germany,” Knewitz says. “We want to make Welzbachtal.”

The Next Great Chardonnay Producers

That confidence is increasingly evident in the glass. Rather than chasing richness or lavish oak, today’s German Chardonnays are defined by energy, tension, and transparency. Matt Turner, wine director at Lei Wine Bar in New York City, consistently finds, “a sort of flinty orange-citrus zest character” running through many of the wines. Chicago sommelier Zach Eastman describes the best examples as combining “an authentically Germanic taut acidity, tension, and minerality” with balanced ripeness and lightness.

There is no single German Chardonnay style, and that may be its greatest strength. “The thing about German Chardonnay is that it doesn’t have to be Burgundy, or Jura for that matter,” says Heather LaVine, owner and wine director of Golden Hour Wine and Quicksand Bar à Vin in Orlando. “It can be its own thing.”

Rather than sharing a rigid stylistic blueprint, LaVine believes the finest iterations are united by an almost unquantifiable sense of energy, one born from thoughtful farming, transparent winemaking, and an honest expression of place.

The cellar has changed, too. “When I was training, I sometimes wondered whether people actually liked Chardonnay or whether they simply liked oaky white wine,” says Carsten Saalwächter of Weingut Saalwächter.

Many modern producers allow fruit, texture, and site to take center stage. Saalwächter jokes that the higher phenolics in his wines give them an edginess, so “you don’t feel as though you’re drinking a lemon cheesecake.”

To appreciate the seriousness of German Chardonnay, “all one has to do is blind taste,” Turner says. I was reminded of that during a visit to Moritz Kissinger, one of Germany’s most exciting Chardonnay producers. Moritz and his wife, Jasmin, poured us a baker’s dozen Chardonnays from some of the world’s finest producers to taste blind. Germany more than held its own. 

It’s easy to see why: these are wines of precision, freshness, and quiet confidence, often offering remarkable value.

“Producing truly great Chardonnay is not the biggest challenge,” says Johannes Kopp of Weingut Kopp in Baden. “Convincing people that Germany belongs among the world’s top Chardonnay producers is.”

After tasting more than 500 German wines this spring, that’s an increasingly difficult argument to dismiss.

title: Is Wine as We Know It on the Brink of Extinction?
summary:
A recent study is sounding the alarm for historic wine regions, if something doesn't change immediately.

The post Is Wine as We Know It on the Brink of Extinction? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Toasting to love and milestones with a glass of Champagne is a relatively ordinary, if elevated and delightful exercise. But it may soon seem as quaint and lovely, but as rare and incompatible with contemporary life as churning butter at home. 

In France and Spain, major portions of wine country went up in flames this summer, echoing an all-too-familiar phenomena haunting countries around the world, every year. Hundreds of thousands of acres of land have been incinerated in Spain and France, with hundreds of thousands of people evacuated from their homes and land. 

When it’s not on fire, it seems like wine country is contending with a deep freeze. This year alone, vineyards across the East Coast and France were devastated by surprise spring freezes and hail events that devastated up to 90% of their potential harvest. If it’s not fires and ice, it’s flooding or drought.  

Direct threats to viticulture from extreme events have moved from once a century ordeals to annual nightmares. But scientists are warning that that harvest damage is the tip of the climate iceberg. A recent study published in Environmental Research Letters warns that it may be too late to save wine grapes—along with other luxury crops like coffee and chocolate—from extinction in some of the regions where they’re currently grown by as early as 2036, unless radical changes are implemented. 

How Climate Change Warps Grape Growth Cycles

While viticulturalists can’t control climate change, or the corporations and governmental policies that many experts warn are actively contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and causing extreme weather events, and an estimated $28 trillion in environmental damage, some researchers and viticulturalists are working to mitigate the effects of climate change they’re already seeing in the way their grapes grow and develop. 

“It’s the extreme heat that worries me most,” admits Jean-François Ott, fourth-generation winemaker at Domaines Ott in Provence. “Above a certain temperature, the vines stop functioning. When I was a child, the harvest began two to three weeks after school started. Today, my children are starting school and we’ve almost finished the harvest. We’ve lost more than a month in 40 years.”

The vine’s growth cycle, Ott says, is also accelerating. 

“We used to have 100 days between flowering and harvest, and today we’re down to 80 days,” Ott says. 

In the face of these stark changes—a reduction of 20% in the time a plant grows has serious implications for the quality of the final product—researchers are turning to geoengineering, like stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), as a potential mitigation. 

“The main idea of SAI is to inject very small, very reflective sulfur dioxide particles into the atmosphere at about 70,000 feet,” says Ariel Morrison, Ph.D., who led the luxury crop study at Colorado State University. “This would create a hazy reflective cloud around the entire planet, which would reflect some sunlight away from the surface and cool the earth.”

Morrison and her colleagues used a climate model to simulate what might happen to temperature, rainfall ,and humidity during the period between 2036 to 2045. SAI can cause temperature to drop,  but it also redistributes heat, rain, and humidity, making it ineffective as a solution in 12 of the 18 major luxury crop regions they studied. Lower temperatures may slash heat stress, but the risk of early winter warmth followed by frost, can’t be guaranteed, which elevates the risk of budbreak damage. 

While Morrison would like to see SAI and other geoengineering solutions, like marine cloud brightening should be studied, she says that without “reducing greenhouse gas emissions” and implementing serious changes in farming practices, wine culture as we know it will be threatened. (Marine cloud brightening is exactly what it sounds like: sea salt particles are sprayed into low-lying marine clouds, which boosts their brightness and reflectivity).

“I think grapes will still grow where they’re currently planted, but whether they will thrive and produce high-quality wine is more questionable,” Morrison says. 

This very pressing problem is top of mind in wine country. 

“Today we’re facing heat levels—even at night—that are forcing us to significantly alter our methods,” Ott says. “Because it takes 10 years from planting to producing a high-quality harvest like the one we aim for, and it’s complicated to completely relocate a vineyard, we’ve significantly adapted our cultivation methods.”

He’s not alone. 

Rethinking Vineyards Spacing and Orientation 

Traditionally, vineyards have been planted to optimize sunlight. But in recent decades, the variety of climate extremes makes that a less sure gamble. 

Being prepared for “anything” motivated the complete replanting initiated at Gloria Ferrer Wines in Sonoma in 2014. They are replanting about 10 acres a year of the 330-acre organically farmed vineyard. 

“As we replant and redevelop our vineyard, we want to be prepared for everything,” says vineyard director Brad Kurtz. “We are purposefully doing everything we can to increase flexibility and long-term resilience.”

One of the biggest forms that’s taking is the team’s decision to change vineyard orientation. 

“We’ve had several crazy heat events that have caused sunburn on Pinot Noir,” Kurtz says. “By changing orientation, it protects the grapes from the harsh afternoon sun. And it coincides with the dominant wind direction, so after excess rain events, the wind dries grapes out and blows off potential disease.”

Adam Casto, head winemaker at Ehlers Estate in Napa, notes that he is currently in the midst of approaching “one of the earliest harvests in recent memory, currently projected to be about two to three weeks ‘early’ of ‘normal.’”

Casto blames the consistently drier, hotter climate conditions, but also “consumer and media trends, globalization, technology, labor, and more.”

Indeed, as wine lovers want fresher and less boozy wines, the climate wants to deliver the opposite. 

Like the team at Gloria Ferrer, Casto and his crew have modified the vineyard design to balance solar irradiance, heat, and water stress. In addition to adjusting row direction and spacing, Casto is experimenting with fruit height and canopy distribution. 

“We are several years into trials with an exciting experimental vine architecture that so far is showing great promise,” Casto says. “We also planted two pilot blocks of Marselan and Arinarora this year to begin learning what other cultivars might be useful in the future as components of our estate.”

Diversifying Grapes and Rootstocks

Experimenting with lesser known, indigenous grape varieties and more resilient rootstocks is a work in progress at many vineyards. 

In Rías Baixas, Spain, winemakers like Emilio Rodríguez Canas at Terras Gauda, are seeing earlier harvest dates consistently. This has pushed them to implement many changes, including seeking out longer-cycle grape varieties that will ripen at “normal” times amid accelerated growing seasons. 

“Caiño Blanco has become a standout variety at Terras Gauda thanks to its very long growing cycle,” Canas explains. “It buds shortly after Albariño and ripens considerably later. With such a long growing cycle, the final part of its ripening takes place in cooler weather with shorter days, which prevents over-ripening and the loss of acidity, important characteristics that have defined our wines for years.”

At Gloria Ferrer, Kurtz says they’ve explored a variety of clones and different rootstocks for their Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, in the hopes of finding great resilience to heat stress and drought. They’ve also created an experimental sparkling Pinot Blanc, brought in Chenin Blanc, and considered using Malvasia Blanc. 

Extreme weather is a bigger problem than early harvests in Mendoza, says Alejandro Vigil, winemaking director at Catena Zapata and co-owner of El Enemigo. And because “every vintage asks different questions,” diversification of everything has become the name of the game. 

“Rather than relying on one solution, we match each variety and farming practice to the specific environment,” he says, noting that their vineyards range from 400 meters to 1,700 meters above sea level. “More than 80% of our Malbec vineyards are planted with massal populations, rather than a single clone. Those populations contain a wide range of genotypes and phenotypes, creating natural diversity within the vineyard. It becomes an insurance policy against uncertainty.”

(Vineyards) Climbing Every Mountain

Insurance is good. 

For every 100 meter increase in elevation, the average temperature decreases by between 0.65 and 1 degrees Celsius. So if a vineyard is 1,000 meters above sea level, it will be up to 10 degrees cooler than a vineyard at sea level. 

Nicolas Catena, Vigil notes, began raising the elevation of vineyards decades ago, before discussing changes in the weather became the opposite of boring. That diversity of vineyard sites, with differences in temperature, solar radiation, water availability, and ripening conditions, allows him to still harvest healthy crops in many places, whether the vintage is hot, cold, dry, and / or wet. 

And while Morrison finds the prospect of higher-elevations promising, she notes there is a built-in limit to the exciting innovation. 

“Expanding to higher elevations or latitudes, which may have previously been too cool to grow grapes, is another option to mitigate the effects of warmer temperatures,” she says, alongside other worthy changes, like planting heat-tolerant grapes and shading vines. “Grapes need a certain amount of sunlight for photosynthesis and polyphenol production, so there’s a limit to the elevation and latitude at which grapes can grow.”

Morrison is also concerned that many of the most impactful interventions are expensive and impossible for smaller producers. She also noted that according to their projections, the likelihood “frost death,” after warm winters produce early buds, which are then demolished by a spring frost, are highest in France, Germany, and northern Spain. 

“Grapes may still generally thrive in these regions, but there could be more years when unexpected frost death wipes out most of a year’s crop,” Morrison says. 

That kind of harvest damage was seen in parts of Europe this spring, with climate’s other vandal, wildfires, finishing the job in France and Spain in July. Grapes will almost surely survive. But their ability to be grown and fermented into something we want to toast to our greatest achievements with will require deep innovation, care, and commitment to sometimes uncomfortable, expensive change. It needs to start now, if not yesterday.

title: How Fires Ravaged One of Europe’s Most Exciting Wine Regions
summary:
The wildfires that swept through Spain's Sierra de Gredos have forced a reckoning on the future of winemaking.

The post How Fires Ravaged One of Europe’s Most Exciting Wine Regions appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When Gearóid Lane finally understood what the fire had done to San Gregorio, there was little left to romanticize.

The vineyard, tucked into the pine forests above El Tiemblo in Spain’s Sierra de Gredos, had vines dating to the 1920s. It was one of the sites around which Lane and his partners built Bodega El Reventón, and the source of one of their two single-vineyard wines. By the time the flames passed, much of the surrounding forest was black and the vineyard had suffered heavy damage.

Still, Lane believes most of the vines will survive.

“With lots of love, hard work, and investment, we will be able to nurse the great majority of the San Gregorio vines back to health,” he says.

Gredos was hardly alone in watching the horizon burn this summer. In late July, enormous fires west of Bordeaux forced mass evacuations and came unnervingly close to one of the world’s most famous wine regions. Bordeaux’s principal appellations escaped direct fire damage, but smoke, extreme heat, and drought have added another layer of uncertainty ahead of an already unusually early harvest.

Days later, the wildfire threat shifted east. Greece battled major fires around Athens and elsewhere in early August, yet another reminder that Europe’s wine regions are entering an era where fire is becoming an increasingly familiar part of the growing season.

But in Gredos, the losses feel particularly cruel because so much of what burns cannot simply be replanted.

Old Vines Up in Smoke

West of Madrid, Garnacha clings to granite and schist slopes at elevation, often in tiny parcels of old bush vines planted 70, 80, sometimes more than 100 years ago. Over the past two decades, those vineyards have attracted a new generation of winemakers drawn by their remarkable transparency and sense of place.

Fernando García of Comando G sees Gredos as far more than a wine region. “Gredos is a spectacular region: a mountainous landscape with wild nature,” he says, “and a long agricultural tradition of vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees. It is an oasis in the middle of the Iberian Peninsula.”

Pete Irvine of PJ Antipoda points to the vines’ deep, established root systems as something that would require decades to recreate.

“The surrounding forest and vegetation like the holm oaks, chestnuts, wild lavender, and juniper give a unique element to the terroir here,” he says. “When those disappear, their recovery also takes decades.”

That is what makes the fires that swept through Gredos in July different from an ordinary bad vintage. The blaze beginning near Burgohondo on July 22 became part of a massive fire complex across Ávila, Madrid, and Toledo that burned tens of thousands of hectares and forced widespread evacuations.

Daniel Ramos, who has made wine in the area since 1999, estimates that 80% of his crop was lost either directly to fire or potentially to smoke. His winery, fortunately, sits inside the town and survived.

At Indiano Winery, Charles Gotchac watched the flames come within roughly 200 meters of the cellar. Friends, neighbors, and firefighters helped defend the property. Some of his vineyards burned; others spent days beneath smoke. “It was a fucking monster,” he recalls.

That smoke now hangs over the coming vintage metaphorically as much as it did physically.

Gotchac expects to confront smoke taint for the first time. Irvine, whose vineyards escaped the flames but not days of lingering smoke, believes that at low levels it could become “a signature of the vintage,” rather than automatically a defect. Campana is less concerned, noting that grapes were still green during the fires and recalling similarly smoky conditions in 2021 that produced no detectable taint.

Yet the longer you speak with Gredos winemakers, the less they talk about smoke taint and the more they talk about the land itself.

The fires that swept through Spain’s Sierra de Gredos exposed not only the vulnerability of one of Europe’s most exciting wine regions, but also a growing consensus among its winemakers that preserving old vines will require rethinking how the entire landscape is managed.

Neglected Land Adding Fuel to the Fire 

Campana remembers a countryside with more people working it, where farmers and shepherds helped maintain the forests. “When you don’t have people living there taking care of stuff, these things are going to happen,” he says. 

Gotchac agrees, arguing that climate change has made fires more intense, but that neglected landscapes often determine how easily they spread.

García takes that idea a step further. “Large wildfires are the result of a combination of human activity and landscapes with huge amounts of unmanaged vegetation,” he says. “All of this is being amplified by climate change: heatwaves, extremely low relative humidity, and strong winds create ideal conditions for fires to develop into massive, uncontrollable blazes.”

Irvine sees the consequences on the ground. Elderly growers become unable to work their vines. Their children have moved to cities. Another historic vineyard is abandoned, vegetation takes over, and a potential firebreak becomes combustible ground.

“Well-managed, tidy ecological vineyards are fire breaks,” he says. “It would be great if that could be more appreciated and country life be more incentivized.”

Ramos is more combative. “If you don’t control a forest, one day or another, it will be so full of rubbish that it will burn in five minutes without any way to control it,” he says.

Ramos, who remembers harvesting Garnacha in mid-September in 1999 and now regularly starts around August 20 to 24, hardly denies that the climate has changed. But like several growers here, he believes hotter, drier conditions have collided with the disappearance of traditional land stewardship.

His immediate concern is not merely his own crop. It is helping elderly growers access subsidies and keep farming.

“If their vineyard keeps alive,” he says, “we will still have some future.”

Lane says producers are now discussing vineyard recovery, fire prevention, and what they should demand from the government. Ramos believes the catastrophe has finally pushed fiercely independent growers toward working together, while Irvine hopes it leads to greater collaboration on farming practices that make the landscape more resilient.

García believes recovery should begin with what the fires spared. “Gredos deserves to be made green,” he says. “Despite the fire, several villages were left untouched, creating green islands that must become the starting point for regeneration.”

When Stubbornness Means Survival

Gredos has never been an easy country. Its vineyards are small, steep, and scattered, surviving largely because generations of stubborn growers believed difficulty was not the same as futility.

And despite everything that burned, none of the growers interviewed for this story spoke of leaving.

Irvine still talks about altitude, granite, old Garnacha and the strange delicacy these brutal mountains can produce.

“Gredos is just getting started,” he says.

Ramos puts it another way. When things become bleak, he says, sometimes you open one of the region’s wines and remember why you stayed in the first place.

“You realize that this can’t disappear.”

title: ‘Tony’ Reminds Us Why We Need to Protect Dive Bars
summary:
Featured in ‘Tony’ and ‘Parts Unknown,’ Bourdain’s favorite Provincetown dive bar has endured for nearly 90 years—and for good reason.

The post ‘Tony’ Reminds Us Why We Need to Protect Dive Bars appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
“Real dive bars aren’t made, they just are,” says Lenny Enos, who runs Old Colony Tap at 323 Commercial St. in Provincetown, Massachusetts. The lawyer-by-day is the third-generation operator of the bar, which has been around for nearly 90 years—including in the mid-’70s, when it was Anthony Bourdain’s favorite dive. In a recent conversation with Wine Enthusiast, Enos reflected on the bar’s role in Tony—and just how little has changed since the late chef and author frequented it.

“The Old Colony is a special place,” he says. “It’s really a throwback in time. It looks essentially the same as it did when Anthony Bourdain would have been in Provincetown, and frankly, the 1950s when my grandfather [Lenny Blue] and his business partner [Herman Jenard] bought the business and redecorated in a nautical theme.” 

With a lifebuoy and a rusty diving helmet, eclectic signage, dark wooden interior, and a ceiling adorned with marine rope and fishing rods, the bar’s decor and bare-bones, unostentatious vibe make it feel authentically divey and nautical. (The jukebox and a Golden Tee 2K arcade game contribute to the overall vintage feel.)

Despite the slow erasure of American dive bar culture, the Old Colony has endured several recessions and global pandemics. With 20 of the 70 dive bars featured in Luke O’Neil’s 2011 book Boston’s Best Dive Bars: Drinking and Diving in Beantown closing by 2016, and California’s historic Clayton Club Saloon shutting down in March 2026 after 153 years, it’s a miracle the Provincetown staple is still standing. 

Clearly, Bourdain wasn’t the only cheap beer aficionado to see something in the cozy dive, but he may have been the most famous. The summer’s hottest biopic is a timely reminder why dive bars are so worth protecting.

A P-Town Institution with Appearances in Parts Unknown and Tony

Director Matt Johnson’s critically-acclaimed biopic Tony, which expands to theaters nationwide on August 21, 2026, spotlights a pivotal season of Bourdain’s youth. 

Co-written by Johnson, Todd Bartels, Lou Howe, and Matthew Miller, Tony depicts a pretentious 19-year-old Bourdain, played by Dominic Sessa (The Holdovers star truly has a look plucked right out of the ‘70s), spending the summer of 1975 in Cape Cod after failing to land a prestigious writing fellowship. “I was—to be frank—a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive, and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking,” reads Bourdain’s best-selling 2000 memoir, Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly, which is the source material for the film. 

An arrogant and unworldly Bourdain follows his crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones), to Provincetown. While she works at Spiritus Pizza, he gets a job in the kitchen of a seafood restaurant called The Flagship, which closed its doors in 2004. Beginning as a grumpy dishwasher, Bourdain is taken under the wing of his head chef (Antonio Banderas) and eventually attends the Culinary Institute of America. 

Shot on location, Tony filmed a bar fight scene in Old Colony Tap, honoring its significance to Bourdain’s P-Town adventures as well as the coastal town’s historic food and drink scene (directly next door, the Lobster Pot opened its doors in 1943). Regardless of the bar’s recent press—which includes A24’s promotional video featuring Johnson and stars Sessa and Leo Woodall enjoying cold beers at the bar—Enos relays that Old Colony is always busy. “Truthfully, I don’t know that it’s really impacted business,” he says, before happily mentioning Sessa called Old Colony’s Bloody Mary one of the best in Massachusetts.

Bourdain’s time spent at Old Colony Tap expands beyond his three summers in Provincetown. He revisited the joint in the 2014 Massachusetts episode of his award-winning travel series Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown. The episode sees Bourdain enjoy Wellfleet oysters, beer, and whisky at the bar, a familiar place he described as “where fishermen eat.” 

Funnily enough, Enos says Old Colony doesn’t serve food. “We don’t have a kitchen. We serve potato chips,” he says. “For the episode, we cooked some of the scallops that they had fished for,” Enos shares, characterizing Bourdain as “super generous and friendly.” He also mentions that a buddy of his, an oyster farmer and fisherman, contributed a fresh bag of oysters just picked from the water. 

Enos even recalls a couple visiting the bar after seeing the Parts Unknown episode. “They told me that first they went to every place that Guy Fieri had been to, and then they ran out of places. So now they were following the places that Anthony Bourdain had been to.”

As American Dive Bar Culture Fades, Old Colony Endures

The dive bar is a significant facet of Americana culture, but it is in decline, as data shows decreases in alcohol consumption and liquor licenses. An August 2025 Gallup poll shows that Americans’ self-reported drinking dropped to 54%, the lowest recorded percentage of alcohol consumers in Gallup’s nearly 90 years of surveying. In the same year, there was a 25% decline in New York alcohol sales, a 40% decline in Philadelphia liquor licenses since 1997, and Chicago businesses with tavern licenses hit a low of 1,200, the number being 3,300 in 1990, as noted by UnHerd. 

The New York Times links dive bar closings to “high rents, rising costs, and a disappearing clientele.” Owner of Manhattan’s Johnny’s Bar, Peter Gonzalez, told the publication that “young kids don’t really drink as much” and “everything’s very corporate now” in the West Village neighborhood. “People want to take a picture of their $20 Cosmo,” he continued, highlighting the modern desire for aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-able craft drinks, which aren’t associated with shabby dives.  

Provincetown being a tiny beach destination as opposed to an increasingly gentrified metropolis may have something to do with the Old Colony’s longevity. From its collection of found beach objects to its loyal patrons, everything about the legendary bar feels organic. After President John F. Kennedy signed the 1961 bill that led to the establishment of the Cape Cod National Seashore, Enos explains that people went for rides on the protected outer beach to scavenge for washed-up objects like buoys, clam rakes, and netting. 

“Somebody would say, ‘I’ll trade you this, give me a $10 tab,’” Enos says of both Old Colony and The Flagship’s dory bar. 

Part of what makes Old Colony a true dive is its inherent nonchalance—it doesn’t even have a website. “There was no—and there remains no—concerted effort to make Old Colony Tap a dive bar. … It just is what it is, and always has been,” Enos says. “When [Bourdain] came back, he mentioned that this is what town was like when he was there in the ‘70s. So much of it has changed, but we’ve just endured.”

Bourdain once said, “My favorite beer is a cold beer, served quickly with minimum fuss,” which parallels Old Colony’s ethos. 

“We don’t do anything special. He wasn’t looking for anything special,” Enos says. So, if you’re looking to order a drink authentic to Bourdain at Old Colony Tap, which offers about 20 different beers, Enos will hand you a shot of Jameson and a draft PBR, or perhaps a can of Narragansett.

title: Wine Always Paid the Bills for This Cattle Rancher. Soon, the Beef Will
summary:
For the first time in at least two generations, the California cattle business should actually make money in 2026. That’s good news for vintner Daniel Sinton.

The post Wine Always Paid the Bills for This Cattle Rancher. Soon, the Beef Will appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If the wine business seems risky and uncertain right now, cattle ranching in California makes it look like child’s play. 

Ever since the industry consolidated around Midwestern meatpackers decades ago, making a buck on beef has been all but impossible for California’s ranchers. Prices rise and mostly fall around unpredictable drought cycles, giving the big processors almost complete dominance over the people who raise the cattle. 

“You live and die by something you can’t control,” says Daniel Sinton, whose family started raising cattle on the oak savannahs of San Luis Obispo County in 1875. “We haven’t made money from cattle in 70 years. We do it because we love the land.” 

They survive because they’re savvy and progressive-minded, empowered by degrees from the University of California, Berkeley (Daniel’s grandfather) and Stanford (he and his dad), which aren’t typical for cowboys. They’ve always treaded lightly on the land, staying abreast of the latest grazing research to efficiently nourish cattle while protecting the landscape. But their smartest move was diversifying into wine by planting Shell Creek Vineyard back in 1972. 

“There was hope that maybe when ranching was down, the vineyard would at least bring in some income to keep us on an even keel,” said Steve Sinton, Daniel’s father. “I would say it’s worked.”

From Cattle to Wine and Back Again

Success didn’t happen immediately. Daniel’s mom, Jane Sinton, hustled to sell the early harvests while simultaneously studying at UC Davis and raising her kids. “I got a million hang-ups,” recalled Jane, who was one of the few women in California wine during those male-dominated days. The vineyard finally became popular when Benziger Family Winery won a big award in Paris for its Shell Creek-grown 1989 Petite Sirah. 

Large-scale contracts paid the bills for decades, but Shell Creek eventually started attracting artisanal winemakers after Broc Cellars in Berkeley sourced its old-vine, own-rooted Chenin Blanc in 2012. Now the vineyard sells Chenin, Valdiguié, Petite Sirah, and Cabernet Sauvignon to 16 clients, from big boys like Duckhorn and Caymus to smaller producers like Thacher, Herman Story, and Outward. “It’s been where the profit is,” said Daniel, who also produces a small label called Avenales Ranch. 

But all that may change this year. For the first time in at least two generations, the California cattle business should actually make money in 2026. Prices are hitting record highs because prolonged droughts in other parts of the country have reduced supplies, and demand has shot up. That’s due to an evolving understanding of both beef in our diets—moderate intake is now considered healthy—and cattle on our landscapes, where grazing animals are increasingly recognized as integral to preserving certain ecosystems. 

“Beef has long been vilified as unhealthy and harmful to the environment,” said Sinton, whose vines benefit from cattle’s poop, urine, and hooves. “A lot of people have realized that is not entirely true.”

He learned as much from his grandfather Jim Sinton, who died in 2017 at 101 while reading a book and drinking Scotch. Toward the end of his life, the family tried to find steaks that reminded Jim of the meat he had eaten decades earlier, but he was never satisfied. So Daniel harvested one of their own grass-raised steers, dry-aged it for 27 days, and served his grandpa a filet. “He took a bite and said, ‘This has the flavor! This is what I used to have!’” recalled Daniel. 

But then he had 400 extra pounds of dry-aged beef on his hands. Daniel offered it to friends via Instagram, and had so many takers that he had to harvest a second animal. It grew by word of mouth into a steady if small business for the Sintons, whose animals were processed at J&R Natural Meats in Paso Robles, one of the only remaining butchers on the entire Central Coast. 

Many other ranchers processed their meat at J&R, so when the butcher closed in 2024, Daniel saw an opportunity. Though they had no plans to enter the butchery business, the Sintons bought the facilities, spruced them up with new equipment, and started cutting everyone’s meat under the name Sinton & Sons.

Setting a New Norm for Ranchers and Processors

The goal is to develop a regional meat market that supports fair rates for ranchers, even when the national prices inevitably dip again. “As the market changes, we’ll be able to buy from producers locally and continue to give them good prices,” said Daniel. “If we can flatten the curve, all of a sudden, cattle become profitable to us again.” 

Like planting Shell Creek 54 years ago, the butcher business is just another smart step in the Sintons’ diversification. Their retail stores in Templeton and Paso Robles have gained loyal fans, and 25 employees at their processing facility are breaking down a handful of cows a day from as far away as Santa Barbara and Temecula. 

Daniel hopes to get up to seven animals a day, which would still make Sinton & Sons an ultrasmall processor. But it’s a move in a better direction, a blip of hope in an otherwise broken system. And, if it works, it’s possible that cattle ranching on the Central Coast could one day even subsidize vineyards. 

“We’re developing a new norm for other producers and us,” he said. “We think that we can create long-term stability for the ranches.”

title: Why Do We Love Tennis Cocktails So Much?
summary:
In part thanks to social media, tennis tournaments have become cocktail hotspots.

The post Why Do We Love Tennis Cocktails So Much? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Ever since 2006, when the Honey Deuce debuted at the U.S. Open, the melon ball-garnished cocktail has reigned as the end-of-summer “it” drink. 

Plastered on social media feeds and the tournament’s live broadcast, the commemorative cocktail became the ultimate flex: holding one demonstrates not only that you’re attending the U.S. Open, but also that you can afford to spend over $20 on a single beverage, maybe multiple. According to Grey Goose, the brand that invented the cocktail with hospitality consultant Nick Mautone, the U.S. Open sold over 740,000 of them in 2025 at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center.

And with over 3.5 million sold since 2011, the Honey Deuce is easily one of the biggest marketing success stories of all time. It should come as no surprise, then, that other brands are searching for their own tennis cocktail virality. 

In 2025, the front-runner was the Watermelon Slice, which will be returning for the 2026 U.S. Open. With a similar fresh fruit appeal, thanks to the watermelon slice garnish, the bubbly Champagne cocktail has a splash of St. Germain, watermelon juice, and bright lime juice to cut through the sweetness. Celebrities like Brittany Snow and Meg Donnelly were photographed sipping it. Like the Honey Deuce, the cocktail is visually striking, served in a fluorescent tennis ball-shaped wine glass, and also like the Honey Deuce, it was a clever feat of marketing. IHG Hotels & Resorts, a sponsor of the U.S. Open, invented the cocktail with optics in mind. 

“The look of the Watermelon Slice alone turns heads,” says Connor Smith, VP of Masterbrand Strategy, IHG Hotels & Resorts. “That neon tennis ball cup is instantly recognizable and makes you do a doubletake. You see it across the grounds and want one in your hand.”

To Ray’s Brooklyn general manager Dylan Wells, it makes perfect sense that the bubbly pink cocktail is this year’s breakout star. “Similarly to the Honey Deuce, the Watermelon Slice has a visual element that’s appealing,” he says. “The tennis-ball yellow glass with the red watermelon garnish makes it Instagram-worthy.” 

It’s possible that the Watermelon Slice’s steep price ($39) also played into its desirability. “The price is part of the appeal as well,” says Nancy Santiago, beverage director at IGC Hospitality Group in New York City. “It offers fans a premium experience that feels special and elevated.

The Honey Deuce Effect

In part thanks to social media, highly visible sporting events have become fodder for cocktail inspiration, as brands try to promote themselves more organically. But it’s not just brands cashing in: bars are putting their own spins on the Honey Deuce and other sports-famous cocktails.

“We have folks requesting Dante’s interpretation of the Honey Deuce all year round,” says Linden Pride, principal of Dante in New York City and London. “It’s been a huge hit for us in London this year also, where we showcased it alongside a Pimms during Wimbledon. All the tennis-inspired drinks have been popular, but folks just love our fluffy melon Honey Deuce.”

Wells says that Ray’s Brooklyn’s Honey Deuce variation was one of their best-selling cocktails last year. “Other tennis tournaments and events have their signature drinks, [but] it feels as though the Honey Deuce reigns supreme over the rest,” says Wells. 

There will only ever be one Honey Deuce, but the Watermelon Slice is a fun end-of-summer treat regardless. Here’s how to make it at home.

title: In Wild Central Sardinia, Rebel Winemakers Are Making Their Mark

Deep in the center of the Mediterranean’s second largest island, the Mamojà Association is pioneering fresher, more dynamic styles of wine.

content:
Traditional winemaking practices, particularly European ones, are like a concrete statue. It begins as wet cement, flexible and malleable, free to take any shape. But over time it hardens into something rigid and stubborn, with any attempt to change its “shape” risking breakage and destruction. But once in a while, change does come along—and often for the better—thanks to rebel-turned-trailblazer winemakers. Consider the “Barolo Boys” of the 1980s and ’90s, who changed Italian wine with their technical innovations born out of economic necessity. Or the Gang of Four, pioneering French producers of Beaujolais who championed organic farming, wild yeasts, and low-intervention methods over industrial bottles made for the mass market. Now, Sardinia has a new crew that’s swinging for the fences. 

Deep in the center of the Mediterranean’s second largest island, Mamoiada is a small village perched in rugged mountains at an elevation of 2,600 feet above sea level. This is a place that rarely has travelers; a Marriott would absolutely be out of the question. But wine-loving tourists might be drawn to the vineyards that surround Mamoiada, dominated by alberello vines that bear Cannonau (the Sardinian name for Grenache), conventionally turned into wines with intense density and alcohol levels that could make anyone anxious if it were sipped next to an open flame. Now fresher, more dynamic, and terroir-driven styles are on the rise in the area, courtesy of 25 winemakers working together as the Mamojà Association.

Paving the Way for a New Kind of Sardinian Wine

Winemaking has been practiced in Mamoiada for centuries. Sardinians have preached for years that this is the birthplace of the Grenache varietal (Spaniards insist they planted it first and have long been known for their Garnacha). Historically speaking, Cannonau often fell into two categories that seem fundamentally opposed. The first is a lean, easygoing style showcased by wines across the entire island, yet one that lacks the “stuffing” that makes it dynamic enough to hold the attention of serious wine drinkers. The second is a highly concentrated style that buries the grapes’ acidity deep inside the finished wine, throwing a veil over the freshness and terroir that the land in Sardinia can really offer. 

Because they belong to an autonomous region of Italy, Sardinians are said to be fiercely independent, distancing themselves so adamantly from mainlanders that they could be called “isolationist.” That stereotype appears to be evolving—at least in the wine scene—as the young winemakers of the Mamojà Association take inspiration from the winemaking world beyond their borders.

Vintners and brothers Simone Sedilesu of Cantina VikeVike and Giovanni Sidulesu of Teularju  grew up in vineyards of the Mamoiada while their grandfather, Guiseppe, brought native varietals back to life. Together, along with Simone’s wife, Francesca Dessolis of ‘Esole winery, they are changing the game quickly while bringing some ride-or-die friends along for the revolution. They’re a pedigreed bunch: Simone worked under the famed Neil Ellis in Stellenbosch, South Africa, where he mastered the essence of exposing the land’s terroir through wine at high elevations. Dessolis worked the vineyards of the Loire Valley and found her way into the holy grail of Burgundy, Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. The combination of their practices from abroad are highly credible for the style forging the new path of the Mamoiada. 

After looking for answers and trying to discover the secrets of what makes for great wine, the two returned home to preach and exercise their findings. While becoming masters of their new craft and attempting to disrupt winemaking in Mamoiada, they ran into an obstacle: Italian wine laws. It turned out that they could not designate a small region around Mamoiada as a new DOC because of the pre-existing Cannonau di Sardegna DOC that stretches across the entire island of Sardinia (usually an area this large falls into the IGT category). That meant any wine they produce in Mamoiada would have to be made in accordance with the extant DOC’s specifications. So they decided to form the Mamojà Association, which will practice as IGT winemaking and allow them to embrace their own path.

New Rules for a New IGT

Among the Association’s core guiding principles: They will grow only Cannonau as their red varietal and Granatza (a rare grape native to the region) as their whites, all cultivated on the region’s 100% granitic soils. Each of the 25 winemakers will use native yeast and allow for spontaneous fermentation while aiming for lower abv levels. This new-school approach allows a sense of total terroir to shine through in their finished wine. Finally the land of each winemaker will focus on specific crus, which they call “ghirada,” just as any other cru or contrada, in order to accentuate the differences between their vineyards and the diversity of the region. The people have responded: Their latest vintages have been enormously successful with the public, wine buyers, and sommeliers alike. 

After hanging out with Simone on a trip to Mamoiada this past April, I found that putting only his own wines in the spotlight was never the main goal; the same goes for his wife, Francesca, and brother, Giovanni. They all wanted the Mamojà Association as a whole to be the focus. This is indicative, in my view, of the courage and selflessness that sustains what they are achieving in the region. The wines of the Mamojà Association speak for themselves; the change in style and appeal of their work are as clear as day. 

It seems that when groups in winemaking stick together and work for something they believe in, great things happen.

Letter from the Publisher

Starry-Eyed Optimism

The future is already here, and it’s not as frightening as it may seem.

The band Wilco has a lyric I think about almost daily: “Come on, children, you’re acting like children. Every generation thinks it’s the end of the world,” Jeff Tweedy croons in “You Never Know.” I’ve come to believe there’s a lot of wisdom packed into that line.

Read More

Lately, it can feel as though every conversation about the future of wine, or life in general, comes wrapped in a sense of impending doom. Whether it’s artificial intelligence, climate change, shifting consumer habits, politics, or economic uncertainty, it’s easy to mistake change for decline. But you won’t find much of that apocalyptic energy in these pages.

This issue is, in many ways, an antidote. Across nearly every profile in the Rising Stars feature, I was struck by the same themes: hospitality, curiosity, and connection. The talented people you’ll meet here aren’t ignoring change; they’re embracing it. They’re finding new ways to build community, preserve authenticity, and invite more people into the world of wine.

Innovation has never been the enemy of tradition. In wine, the two have always evolved together. Every generation inherits remarkable traditions, and every generation is responsible for finding new ways to keep them alive.

That’s exactly what this year’s Rising Stars are doing. They’re proving that what makes wine special isn’t changing. The ways we discover it, share it, and experience it are. And that’s something worth celebrating—no hand- wringing needed.

Each generation is confronted with its own version of a crisis. The successful ones look at it through the lens of possibility.

I hope these stories inspire you to do the same.
